extracted.intended_audience: law students and patent practitioners (IP lawyers, patent examiners)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether claimed inventions (especially computer-implemented and business-method claims) satisfy 35 U.S.C. § 101 using the Alice/Mayo framework and related PTO guidance; focuses on identifying abstract ideas and any 'inventive concept' or practical application that makes a claim patent-eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayo two-step framework
rubrics_metrics.description: First, determine whether the claims at issue are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea). If so, ask, 'what else is there in the claims before us?' and consider the elements of each claim both individually and 'as an ordered combination' to determine whether the additional elements 'transform the nature of the claim' into a patent-eligible application by supplying an 'inventive concept.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step two is described as a search for an 'inventive concept'—an element or combination of elements that is 'sufficient to ensure that the patent in practice amounts to significantly more than a patent upon the [ineligible concept] itself.' Use precedents (Benson, Flook, Diehr) to apply the framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of an 'abstract idea'
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite fundamental economic practices or methods of organizing human activity (e.g., intermediated settlement, hedging) or basic algorithms/mathematical concepts can be 'abstract ideas' and therefore patent-ineligible under § 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare claimed concept to prior Supreme Court examples (e.g., Benson, Flook, Bilski, Diehr). If the claim depicts a building-block activity long prevalent in commerce (e.g., 'intermediated settlement'), treat it as an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption concern as the core §101 rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: The exclusion for laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas is driven by a concern about pre-emption—monopolization of basic tools of scientific and technological work that would impede innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating eligibility, assess whether the claim would 'disproportionately tie up' the underlying building-block idea; claims that risk broad preemption are suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere recitation of a generic computer is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Stating an abstract idea 'while adding the words "apply it with a computer"' or reciting implementation on a generic computer does not transform an abstract idea into a patent-eligible invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Benson and Flook: implementing an abstract algorithm or idea on existing computers is not enough. Diehr shows eligibility exists only where the claim improves a technological process rather than merely invoking a computer. The computer must do more than perform well-understood, routine, conventional activities specified at a high level of generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional/generic hardware claiming does not confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: System claims that recite 'specific hardware' only in purely functional and generic terms (e.g., 'data processing system,' 'communications controller,' 'data storage unit') do not add a meaningful limitation beyond implementation via computers and therefore do not make an abstract idea patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether recited hardware offers a meaningful limitation beyond generally linking the method to a technological environment. If nearly any computer could perform the recited functions, the hardware is likely conventional and not an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept must be more than conventional activity
rubrics_metrics.description: At Mayo step two, additional features must 'add a specific limitation or combination of limitations that are not well-understood, routine, conventional activity in the field,' indicating an inventive concept; merely appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities at a high level of generality is indicative that an inventive concept is not present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess each additional element for novelty and whether it meaningfully limits the claim beyond the abstract idea. The PTO guidance explicitly frames this as the dividing test for 'inventive concept.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Diehr principle — improvement to technology can render claims eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that use an abstract mathematical formula or idea but apply it in a process that solves a technological problem or improves an existing technological process (e.g., Diehr's curing-of-rubber process) can be patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for claims that effect an improvement in computer functioning or another technological field (not merely use a computer as a tool). The claimed invention should do more than implement a business practice on a computer; it should solve a technological problem in a non-conventional way.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance (2019) — practical application prong
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO added a prong to the first step of the Mayo test: if the claim recites a judicial exception and is 'integrated into a practical application,' then it is patent-eligible and the PTO does not proceed to Mayo step two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the guidance, determine whether the claim integrates the judicial exception into a practical application; if so, eligibility is established at step 1. Otherwise, proceed to evaluate whether additional elements supply an inventive concept (see the two bullet tests). Empirical evidence indicates the 2019 guidance lowered initial rejections and decreased examiner variability in 'Alice-affected' areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three PTO-drawn categories of 'abstract ideas'
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO distilled 'abstract ideas' into three groups: (1) Mathematical concepts (relationships, formulas, calculations); (2) Certain methods of organizing human activity (fundamental economic principles/practices, commercial/legal interactions, managing personal behavior/relationships); (3) Mental processes (observations, evaluations, judgments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing claims, map claimed subject matter to one of these three groups as part of determining whether a judicial exception is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business method and internet-centric claims — factual/claim-specific inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all software- or Internet-related claims are ineligible. A claim that merely recites a business practice performed on the Internet (or routine Internet use) is likely abstract, whereas claims that are 'necessarily rooted in computer technology' to overcome a problem specifically arising in computer networks may have an 'inventive concept' sufficient for eligibility (e.g., DDR Holdings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claimed solution addresses a technical problem particular to computer networks or whether it merely applies a pre-Internet business practice on the Internet. Courts (and the PTO) examine prior cases to find analogous reasoning when a universal definition of 'abstract idea' is elusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that 'merely describe a method of doing business' are suspect under §101
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that 'merely describes a method of doing business' may not qualify as a 'process' under §101 and can be treated as an abstract idea (as noted in concurring/dissenting opinions like Bilski and Sotomayor's concurrence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat pure business-method claims skeptically: unless tied to a technological improvement or a practical application beyond conventional computer implementation, they are likely to be deemed ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-law comparative methodology for defining 'abstract idea'
rubrics_metrics.description: Because a single universal definition of 'abstract idea' is difficult, courts examine earlier cases with similar descriptive natures—what prior cases were about and how they were decided—to determine whether a claim is an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogies to Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedents (Benson, Flook, Diehr, Bilski, Alice, Ultramercial, DDR Holdings, Amdocs) to situate the claim and predict eligibility outcomes rather than relying on a single testable definition.
